The simpler forms of Chinese characters that the People's Republic of China made standard from 1956, to help spread reading and writing. They are now used in mainland China, Singapore and Malaysia, while Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau keep the traditional forms.

Reformers had long argued that complex characters held China back. Some radicals of the May Fourth era even wanted to replace them with an alphabet. After the communist victory of 1949, a reform committee under Mao Zedong chose to simplify instead. The 1956 scheme cut the number of strokes in hundreds of common characters, often using shorthand forms already in handwriting for centuries, and merged some characters into one. The Pinyin system of writing Chinese in Latin letters was adopted in 1958 alongside it, as an aid to learning.

A second round of simplification in 1977 went too far and was withdrawn. Literacy in China rose from a minority of adults in 1949 to almost all young people today. Japan made its own, smaller simplification after 1945.
